Volume 08 · Chapter 08

Real options and investment timing

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c07

By the endValue flexibility and identify where static NPV understates contingent choices.

Capability and prerequisites

You can value a feasible sequence of investment decisions, distinguish a forecast from a pricing rule, and explain what an option calculation adds to an ordinary NPV. Use the incremental cash-flow discipline of Chapter 1, the dated valuation rules of Chapter 2, the financing constraints of Chapter 6, and the valuation comparisons of Chapter 7. Conditional probability and Bayes' rule were taught in Volume 3; the small option-pricing argument needed here is derived below. The later derivatives volume is an extension, not a prerequisite.

Tern Thermal Systems can build a line immediately, reserve a site and decide later, or run a pilot before committing the remaining budget. A spreadsheet containing one unchangeable production forecast cannot compare those policies. The relevant object is a policy: an action for each information set the decision maker could actually reach. A real option is a feasible right to change an operating or investment decision. It need not be a traded security, and a managerial wish without access, permission, time or financing is not such a right.

All businesses, contracts, probabilities and amounts below are original fictional teaching inputs. Money is thousands of currency units (kCU); rates are effective rates per one-year interval. Each worked case is a separate proposal, not an additive division of one company. Taxes and other claims are already absent from, or incorporated in, the stipulated net amounts. No case supplies current market data or an actual legal entitlement.

1. Specify the right before assigning it a value

An investment is irreversible to the extent its cost cannot be recovered after commitment. The possibility of learning before that commitment can matter even when building now has positive NPV. Conversely, waiting can forfeit operating receipts, a customer, a permit or the right itself. A useful contract description identifies who controls the action, what can be acquired or surrendered, the exercise cost, the last decision date, what information arrives beforehand, and competing actions that exercise rules prohibit.

Different operating rights require different comparisons
RightDecision at the relevant dateCost or constraint to retain
DelayInvest now, preserve a later choice, or let the opportunity lapseLost interim operations, expiry, reservation costs and competition
ExpandPay additional investment for additional operating cashIncremental working capital, installation time and financing capacity
AbandonCompare continuing value with net disposal proceedsClosure costs, taxes, obligations and possible loss of expansion rights
StageFund a limited phase, observe its result, then fund or stop a later phaseFirst-stage spending is lost even when the later phase is rejected

Static NPV here means the value of a specified fixed policy minus its investment cost. Discounted cash-flow analysis can also value a contingent policy if the cash-flow model and risk treatment reflect its choices. It is the restriction to an unchangeable policy, not discounting itself, that can omit flexibility. A separate option premium is appropriate only when the base valuation excludes that same flexibility. These distinctions are the chapter's own bookkeeping rules; the source route on real options discusses delay, expansion, abandonment and the practical limits of assigning value to such rights. [Real-option applications and limits]

2. Backward induction respects information and timing

A decision node lists actions currently available. A chance node lists possible next observations. Start at the final date, value the remaining choices there, and work backward. For a node n at date t, write A(n) for its feasible actions, c(n,a) for current net cash, and V(m) for the optimized value at a possible next node m. With a justified linear valuation rule represented by positive one-period state prices π(m|n),

V(n) = maxa ∈ A(n) { c(n,a) + Σm π(m|n,a)V(m) }.

A state price is the current value of one unit paid in a specified next state. If the conditional risk-free rate is r and the pricing weights are q, then π = q/(1+r), with the weights summing to one. Actions can change the subsequent states or probabilities, so those changes belong in the tree. A node value already includes subsequent cash; do not add those same receipts again at its parent. A current outlay enters c with a negative sign. A future outlay must be discounted from its actual date.

The maximization must occur at the information set where the action is chosen. If two future states are still indistinguishable when a decision is due, the action must be the same in both. Taking the better action separately in those unobserved states grants the firm information it does not possess. At an observed state, however, forbidding a feasible response understates its choices.

There are two different valuation foundations in this chapter. The first worked case derives market state prices from traded spanning claims: portfolios that reproduce every relevant payoff. The other cases explicitly adopt a risk-neutral owner's decision criterion, expected dated money discounted at a stated time-preference rate, with sufficient wealth and linear utility over these outcomes. In those cases physical probabilities enter the owner's objective. That assumption supplies a decision value, not evidence that actual investors would pay it. With risk-averse owners or unspanned project risk, use an appropriate utility model or justified pricing kernel and recognize the resulting model dependence. A convenient physical forecast and a risk-free rate alone do not establish market value.

3. Price a simple delay right by replication

Suppose a traded operating clone costs S0 now and has two possible date-1 values Su and Sd, with Su > Sd. It pays no interim cash. Borrowing and lending at the same certain rate r, fractional trading and short sales are available without taxes, fees or default. Both states are possible. A date-1 claim pays Cu or Cd. Hold Δ units of the clone and B in the date-0 risk-free account; negative B means borrowing. Matching both payoffs requires

ΔSu + (1+r)B = Cu,   ΔSd + (1+r)B = Cd.

Subtract the equations to obtain Δ = (Cu−Cd)/(Su−Sd), then B = (Cd−ΔSd)/(1+r). Equal replicable payoffs must have the same market value; otherwise buying the cheaper package and selling the dearer one yields current cash and no future net liability. Thus C0 = ΔS0+B. Rearranging our two equations gives

q = [(1+r)S0−Sd]/(Su−Sd),   C0 = [qCu+(1−q)Cd]/(1+r).

The no-arbitrage condition Sd < (1+r)S0 < Su ensures 0 < q < 1. Outside it, the specified tradable clone and bond already admit arbitrage. The quantity q is a risk-neutral pricing weight, not the analyst's physical probability of an up state. The local derivation follows the replication principle taught in MIT's options lecture; the examples and algebraic verification here are original. [Replication reference]

Worked example 1 — Tern's exclusive one-year construction right

The clone costs 100 now and will be worth 145 or 70 at date 1. These are values of the remaining operating claim at that date, not one year's sales. The clone can be traded or liquidated at those values. The risk-free rate is 5%. Tern already owns a right to pay 90 either now or at date 1 for an identical operating claim. There is no interim production cash, the right is exclusive until its date-1 expiry, the 90 cost is unchanged, and funds are available for exercise. The real project's terminal claim is perfectly spanned by the clone.

Immediate investment has NPV 100−90 = 10. Waiting permits investment in the up state and rejection in the down state: the date-1 net payoffs are 55 and 0. The pricing weight is (105−70)/(145−70) = 7/15. The delay right is worth (7/15)×55/1.05 = 220/9 = 24.444444 at date 0. With both dates available, choose the larger of 10 and 24.444444, so wait. The gain relative to mandatory immediate investment is 14.444444. The whole 24.444444 is the opportunity's value before any new rights fee; adding it to the immediate NPV would count the opportunity twice.

Replication verifies the result directly. Buy 11/15 of the clone and borrow 440/9 = 48.888889. The borrowed amount grows to 154/3. The up payoff is (11/15)×145−154/3 = 55; the down payoff is (11/15)×70−154/3 = 0. Its initial cost is (11/15)×100−440/9 = 220/9.

A physical up probability of 0.6 implies expected clone value 115 and a 15% expected clone return. It implies expected option payoff 33. Discounting 33 at 5% gives 31.428571; discounting it at the clone's 15% gives 28.695652. Both miss the replication value. The option's own expected return is 33/(220/9)−1 = 35%. A nonlinear exercise rule changes risk exposure; copying the underlying asset's expected return is not a valid shortcut.

Now change the contract: immediate construction also earns a certain date-1 interim receipt D, whereas delayed construction misses it. The remaining clone still has the same 145/70 values. The immediately acquired package is now worth 100+D/1.05, not 100. For D = 20, immediate NPV is 29.047619, exceeding waiting value. The switching point solves 10+D/1.05 = 220/9, giving D = 91/6 = 15.166667. This is an opportunity-cost comparison, not a general rule to postpone every positive-NPV project.

Before acquiring either right, subtract its acquisition fee at the date paid and compare the best attainable policy with the outside alternative. If a rights fee has already been irreversibly paid, it is sunk for the exercise decision but remains part of the original investment's realized economics. A private project without a traded clone cannot inherit this exact replication price merely because its forecast has two branches. The nontraded-asset and uncertain-exclusivity caveats are explicit in the real-options source. [Scope of market pricing]

4. Expansion and abandonment are a feasible menu

At a decision date, compare all alternatives in currency of that date. If continuing a base operation is worth V, an optional expansion adds operating value X at additional cost K, and abandoning yields net proceeds L, then the menu may be {V, V+X−K, L}. Its value is the maximum of those alternatives. Net disposal proceeds must include cleanup, closure, tax and other obligations that belong to the owner. They are not automatically the asset's accounting book value. Expansion adds incremental cash and costs; it does not replace the base by the expansion's gross revenue.

Worked example 2 — Choose a response after demand is observed

A separate Tern facility costs 70 at date 0. At date 1 high or low demand is observed, with physical probabilities 0.4 and 0.6. The owner explicitly uses linear expected money and a 5% annual discount rate. The following figures are date-1 monetary equivalents of all remaining net operating cash under that same criterion. There is no earlier operating cash. Expansion is immediate and fully fundable; abandonment and expansion cannot both be chosen.

Date-1 alternatives, kCU
Observed stateContinue baseExpansion's gross incrementExpansion costContinue plus expandNet abandonment
High120603514565
Low4012351765

The fixed base policy is worth (0.4×120+0.6×40)/1.05 = 68.571429, so its NPV is −1.428571. The flexible policy expands after high demand and abandons after low demand. Its gross value is (0.4×145+0.6×65)/1.05 = 92.380952, and its NPV is 22.380952. The value added by these free, owned rights is 23.809524.

Relative to the base, expansion alone adds 0.4×25/1.05 = 9.523810; abandonment alone adds 0.6×25/1.05 = 14.285714. They add exactly here because they improve different states and leave the other action's opportunity unchanged. That is a property of this particular table. If expansion and abandonment both improve the same state but are mutually exclusive, adding their separate premiums overstates their joint value. Exercise 4 checks this failure.

The low-state sale is triggered by 65 > 40, not by the original 70 cost. Spending 70 is relevant at date 0; once spent, it is not a new cost of continuing at date 1. The table's operating values also need not be cash in the bank. If expansion cannot be financed, remove it from the feasible menu and recompute.

5. Staged investment buys a decision, not a guaranteed success

A development gate limits the money committed before technical or commercial information arrives. Earlier spending can create the technical capability as well as the information. Separate that enabling investment from a pure research report. A project with several gates is valued from the final gate backward; each early decision includes the optimized continuation value it makes accessible. A shutdown option does not refund the earlier failed experiment.

Worked example 3 — A technical pilot and a scale-up gate

A pilot costs 12 now. At date 1 it is validated with probability 0.6; otherwise it fails. This pilot is technically required before any scale-up. A validated design can be scaled for 30 at date 1 to receive 80 at date 2; after failure the same scale-up cost produces zero. There is no salvage. The owner uses linear expected money at 10% per year, knows the validation result before scale-up, and can fund either choice.

At a successful gate, continuation NPV is 80/1.1−30 = 470/11 = 42.727273. At a failed gate it is −30, so stop and retain zero continuation value. The staged proposal's date-0 NPV is −12+0.6×(470/11)/1.1 = 1368/121 = 11.305785. This calculation discounts the scale-up spending for one year and the final receipt for two.

For a controlled comparison, a forced-completion contract has the same pilot and outcomes but obliges the owner to spend 30 at date 1 even after failure. Its NPV is −12−30/1.1+0.6×80/1.1² = 48/121 = 0.396694. The stop right adds 120/11 = 10.909091, exactly the PV of the 30 expenditure avoided with probability 0.4. It does not add the entire staged value on top of a forecast that already excludes failed scale-ups.

If the validation probability is p, beginning the pilot is worthwhile when −12+p(470/11)/1.1 ≥ 0, or p ≥ 363/1175 = 0.308936. Above this threshold the rule is still conditional: scale only validated designs. Technical validation is the only remaining uncertainty in this deliberately small case; commercial demand risk would require additional branches.

6. Value information against the best uninformed policy

Information is useful because it can change an action. A more accurate forecast need not be worth buying if the same decision remains optimal. For a fixed decision date, fixed action set and linear monetary criterion, let N(a,s) be an action's dated net value in state s. Without a new signal, choose maxaΣsp(s)N(a,s). With a signal y, first update beliefs, then choose maxaΣsp(s|y)N(a,s), and average over the signals that might arrive. Gross expected value of sample information, EVSI, is the second value minus the first, before any information fee.

Why is this difference nonnegative? The informed decision maker can use the old action after every signal. Averaging those conditional expected payoffs reproduces the old unconditional payoff. Optimizing after each signal can only improve it. If the true state is revealed before choice, the decision maker can attain Σsp(s)maxaN(a,s). This is at least as large as the payoff from any signal-based policy, so 0 ≤ EVSI ≤ EVPI, the value of perfect information, under the same dates, rights and criterion. These statements exclude fees and harmful changes to the opportunity itself. With nonlinear utility, an expected-utility improvement must be converted to a willingness-to-pay by putting the fee inside utility; utility points are not currency. [Decision-analysis reference]

Worked example 4 — An imperfect report before a fixed launch date

A separate product can be launched only at date 1, at cost 60, for a date-2 receipt of 160 if demand is good and 40 if bad. The physical prior probability of good demand is 0.4. The owner uses linear expected money at 10% per year. A report purchased now is delivered just before the date-1 launch decision. It changes neither the actual demand distribution nor the launch date, cost or available capacity. Its positive-report probability is 0.75 under good demand and 0.25 under bad demand.

Without a report, expected receipt is 0.4×160+0.6×40 = 88. At date 1 launch has expected NPV 88/1.1−60 = 20, so launch. Its date-0 decision value is 200/11 = 18.181818. Comparing the report only with rejection would give the wrong baseline.

A positive report has probability 0.4×0.75+0.6×0.25 = 0.45. Bayes' rule gives P(good|positive) = 0.30/0.45 = 2/3. A negative report has probability 0.55 and posterior good probability 0.10/0.55 = 2/11. The conditional expected date-2 receipts are respectively 120 and 680/11. Their date-1 launch NPVs are 540/11 = 49.090909 and −460/121 = −3.801653. Therefore launch only after a positive report.

The gross date-0 value with the report is 0.45×(540/11)/1.1 = 2430/121 = 20.082645. Subtracting the best no-report value yields EVSI = 230/121 = 1.900826. A report fee of 1 paid now is worthwhile: net proposal value becomes 19.082645, a gain of 0.900826. A fee of 3 is too high. Paying for the report does not eliminate the possibility of a loss after a false positive.

Perfect information would permit launch only in the good state. Gross date-0 value would be 0.4×(160/1.1−60)/1.1 = 3760/121 = 31.074380, giving EVPI = 1560/121 = 12.892562. It is an upper bound on the gross value of a report under the same opportunities, not a forecast of what this imperfect report will deliver. The fee threshold is 1.900826, not 12.892562.

7. Identify what changes the decision

More time can expand a choice set when everything else is fixed, but actual extensions can cost money, lose customers or expose the project to entry. A rival's action can change future operating value or whether the right survives; strategic competition may require a game rather than an exogenous chance branch. Installation lags also matter: learning at expiry is useless if construction had to begin earlier. A permit that expires before the modeled exercise date is not the modeled right.

A larger feasible action set cannot reduce optimized value when the additional choices are free and may be ignored. This does not imply that purchasing the rights is profitable, that increasing every form of uncertainty increases enterprise value, or that shareholders can finance the maximizing action. A spread in a fixed underlying payoff can raise a convex option payoff's expectation while simultaneously reducing operating cash, changing market risk or increasing required investment. State exactly what is held fixed in a sensitivity calculation.

For a valuation memo, give the fixed-policy baseline, actual information dates, feasible contingent policy, pricing or preference rule, and incremental cost of the rights. Reconcile the flexible forecast with the DCF or comparable value already in use. Then test the assumptions that could reverse the policy: lost interim cash, entry, signal accuracy, salvage obligations, capital availability and delays. A sensitivity table can expose uncertainty; it cannot certify a guessed spanning relation or turn physical probabilities into risk-neutral weights.

Reproducible decision laboratory

The original input file, standard-library Python program and timing and model guide reproduce all four cases without a network connection. Put the input and program in the same directory and run python3 v08-c08-analysis.py. The reference output records exact fractions and decimals. The lab keeps market replication separate from the explicitly stipulated owner criterion; it does not estimate a real project's price.

First verify the two replicated payoffs. Then change the interim receipt, remove expansion funding, alter validation probability, and change the report's likelihoods. Explain which decision changes before reading the new output. Treat a report with identical likelihoods in both demand states as uninformative. The input validator rejects invalid probabilities, a market clone inconsistent with strict no-arbitrage, and attempts to label the owner cases as market-priced without adding a pricing model.

Practice

  1. A traded clone costs 80, has date-1 values 120 or 60, pays no interim cash, and can be traded under the replication assumptions above. The annual risk-free rate is 5%. An owned right allows investment for 90 now or at date 1. Find the pricing weight, waiting value, replicating holdings and optimal timing. If the physical up probability is 0.5, compute the clone's and the waiting claim's expected returns.
  2. Return to Worked example 1. Immediate construction earns an additional certain interim receipt of 10 at date 1; delay misses it. Find the immediately acquired package's value, immediate NPV and preferred policy. If an otherwise unavailable right to choose either date costs 4 now, with rejection worth zero, is acquiring it worthwhile? Distinguish that acquisition decision from the later exercise decision after the fee has been paid.
  3. Reconstruct Worked example 2's base and flexible NPVs without using its reported totals. Identify the realized date-1 actions and value each right separately. Explain why the original 70 cost should not make the manager retain the facility after low demand.
  4. In Worked example 2, replace only the low-state expansion terms: its gross increment is 50 and its cost is 20. The high-state row is unchanged. What is the low-state optimal value? Show the error from adding separate expansion and abandonment premiums to the base in that state. What if the low-state expansion decision must instead be committed before the high/low demand observation—can the firm still use the same state-by-state maximization without additional analysis?
  5. A technical pilot costs 15 now and validates with probability 0.5 at date 1. Scale-up costs 40 at date 1; its date-2 receipt is 90 after validation and zero after failure. Use the stated linear-owner criterion at 10%. Calculate the staged NPV, forced-completion NPV, value of the stopping right and minimum validation probability for beginning the pilot.
  6. For Worked example 4, derive the minimum posterior good-demand probability that makes launch worthwhile. Verify both posterior decisions and the exact maximum date-0 report fee. Replace the likelihoods by P(positive|good) = P(positive|bad) = 0.5. Find the two posteriors and the report's gross information value.
  7. A private nontradable opportunity is forecast to have date-1 operating values 145 and 70 with physical up probability 0.6. It may be acquired at date 1 for 90. There is no observed date-0 clone price and no spanning security, utility function or project risk premium. Does a 5% risk-free rate identify the waiting right's market value? Illustrate non-identification with positive hypothetical pricing weights 0.3 and 0.7, then explain what extra assumption would justify using the physical probability.
  8. A memo for Worked example 2 already values the optimized 145/65 state outcomes at 92.380952, then adds a 23.809524 flexibility premium, subtracts 70 initial cost and subtracts a 3 date-0 rights fee. Repair the calculation. Now assume that after the initial investment and fee, only 30 of date-1 cash is available for expansion and no additional financing or pledge of continuation value is possible. Abandonment remains feasible. Recompute the feasible policy's NPV net of the same fee. State two factual checks needed before treating either answer as a business valuation.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The pricing weight is (84−60)/(120−60) = 0.4. Exercise payoffs are 30 and 0; waiting value is 0.4×30/1.05 = 80/7 = 11.428571. Δ = 30/60 = 1/2; B = −30/1.05 = −200/7 = −28.571429. Initial replication cost is 40−200/7 = 80/7. Final payoffs are 60−30 = 30 and 30−30 = 0. Immediate NPV is −10, so wait, exercising only after the up state. The clone's physical expected value is 90, giving expected return 12.5%. The waiting claim's expected payoff is 15, so its expected return is 15/(80/7)−1 = 31.25%. Neither physical return replaces the pricing-weight calculation arbitrarily.

  2. The immediate package is worth 100+10/1.05 = 109.523810; immediate NPV is 19.523810. Waiting remains worth 24.444444, so choose waiting. The acquired choice is worth max(19.523810,24.444444)−4 = 20.444444 versus rejection at zero: buy it under the stated assumptions. Once 4 is irrevocably paid, comparing the two exercise policies uses their remaining values. Subtracting the fee from only the waiting branch would wrongly make the sunk acquisition cost determine timing. The fee still belongs in the original proposal's total NPV.

  3. Base expected date-1 value is 0.4×120+0.6×40 = 72; NPV is 72/1.05−70 = −10/7 = −1.428571. The high-state menu selects 145 from {120,145,65}; the low-state menu selects 65 from {40,17,65}. Expected optimized value is 97; NPV is 97/1.05−70 = 470/21 = 22.380952. Expansion alone adds 0.4×25/1.05 = 200/21 = 9.523810; abandonment alone adds 0.6×25/1.05 = 100/7 = 14.285714. At the low node, keeping the facility sacrifices net sale proceeds 65 to retain a claim worth 40. The already-paid 70 is identical under both choices and cancels. Its loss does not justify a further loss of 25.

  4. Low-state expansion now gives 40+50−20 = 70, exceeding base 40 and abandonment 65, so expand. The separate gains over base are 30 and 25; adding both to 40 produces 95, overstating the attainable 70 by 25. With the original 0.6 low probability, the date-0 overstatement is 0.6×25/1.05 = 14.285714. The full flexible policy now has outcomes 145 and 70, value 100/1.05 = 95.238095 and NPV 25.238095. If expansion must be committed before observing demand, the chosen commitment must be the same in indistinguishable future states. Its cost, state-dependent consequences and interaction with later abandonment must be specified at that earlier node. The old observed-state menu cannot silently be reused; it grants unavailable information. A good answer explains the information restriction rather than inventing an unspecified early contract.

  5. Successful continuation is 90/1.1−40 = 460/11 = 41.818182; failed continuation is rejected. Staged NPV is −15+0.5×(460/11)/1.1 = 485/121 = 4.008264. Forced completion is −15−40/1.1+0.5×90/1.1² = −1715/121 = −14.173554. The difference is 200/11 = 18.181818, equal to 0.5×40/1.1, the avoided failed scale-up. Beginning the pilot requires −15+p(460/11)/1.1 ≥ 0, so p ≥ 363/920 = 0.394565. Paying the pilot's 15 only on successful paths would be a timing and selection error.

  6. For posterior p, date-1 launch NPV is (40+120p)/1.1−60. It is nonnegative when 40+120p ≥ 66, or p ≥ 13/60 = 0.216667. The positive posterior 2/3 passes; the negative posterior 2/11 ≈ 0.181818 fails. The report's gross proposal value is 2430/121, while the best no-report proposal is 2200/121. Therefore its maximum date-0 fee is 230/121 = 1.900826, with indifference at equality. If both likelihoods are 0.5, both posteriors equal the prior 0.4. Launch after either report; the expected policy and value are unchanged, so EVSI = 0. A nonzero fee would then reduce value.

  7. No unique market value follows. Terminal exercise payoffs are 55 and zero, but their state prices remain unspecified. Weight 0.3 with a 5% risk-free rate gives 0.3×55/1.05 = 110/7 = 15.714286; weight 0.7 gives 110/3 = 36.666667. Both proposed state-price pairs are positive and price a certain unit at 1/1.05; nothing in the stated traded data selects between them. They would imply different prices for the underlying claim, which is precisely why omitting an observed spanning price matters. Using physical p = 0.6 would give 220/7 = 31.428571 under a stipulated linear-owner criterion at 5%, or under a separately justified market model that actually equates those pricing and physical probabilities. A physical forecast alone establishes neither premise. If the original traded clone price of 100 were restored, its no-arbitrage restriction would instead identify q = 7/15.

  8. The 92.380952 already includes the flexibility. Correct unconstrained NPV after the rights fee is 92.380952−70−3 = 19.380952. Adding 23.809524 again has no separate cash-flow basis. With only 30 available and no other funding, expansion costing 35 is infeasible. Choose base continuation 120 after high demand and abandonment 65 after low demand. Expected date-1 value is 0.4×120+0.6×65 = 87; net NPV is 87/1.05−70−3 = 69/7 = 9.857143. The available-cash statement applies after the initial investment and fee; those earlier costs do not need to be subtracted from 30 again. Suitable factual checks include the owner's actual valuation criterion or market pricing evidence; the timing and availability of funding; the right to abandon and its net obligations; the reliability of state values and probabilities; and whether the base forecast already optimizes operations. At least two must be tied to how they could change the result.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back: In two minutes, explain why “a positive NPV means invest immediately” can fail, and why “more uncertainty makes the company more valuable” also fails. Use the owned delay right, lost interim receipts and one constraint on exercise.

Expected explanation

A positive immediate NPV compares investing now with rejecting. An owned right can offer a better policy: wait, learn, and invest only in favorable states. In the original delay case, waiting is worth 24.444444 versus immediate NPV 10. But a certain lost interim receipt of 20 raises the immediate policy's NPV to 29.047619, reversing the choice. These comparisons require a real, funded right and a compatible valuation model. More dispersion may improve a particular convex option payoff when other inputs are held fixed; it can also lower the underlying business's expected cash or remove financing. Company value therefore has no blanket monotonic relationship with uncertainty.

Delayed check: A week later, reconstruct the replication equations and the date ordering of the pilot without opening the chapter. Then state the correct baseline for an information purchase and explain when maximizing separately in future states is invalid.

Retention answer

Matching two payoffs gives Δ(Su−Sd) = Cu−Cd and (1+r)B = Cd−ΔSd; initial value is ΔS0+B. For the pilot, pay 12 at date 0, observe validation at date 1, pay 30 only after success, then receive 80 at date 2. Compare information with the best feasible policy without that information, not automatic rejection. State-specific maximization is invalid when the action is due before the states can be distinguished. Rework Exercises 1, 5 and 6 if any date, baseline or information restriction is missing.

Sources and next steps

MIT's options lecture provides a route to binomial replication and its assumptions; Damodaran's real-options paper discusses operating applications and limits of applying traded-option models to projects; Duke's decision-analysis handout distinguishes information value, posterior decisions and utility-based willingness to pay. These are scoped method references, not sources of the chapter's fictional companies, cases or exercises. Original calculations are reconstructed in the lab and reviewed separately.

The later options and binomial-replication chapter develops a broader derivatives toolkit. The next corporate-finance chapter applies valuation discipline to mergers and acquisitions, where promised synergies and strategic opportunities must likewise be tied to feasible incremental cash and costs.

Sources and further study

  • Andrew W. Lo, MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I — Lectures 10–11: Options (Fall 2008) — Scoped primary teaching reference for two-state replication, its trading assumptions, equal-payoff pricing and independence of the pricing formula from the physical state probability. Original chapter derives and verifies its own numerical contracts.
  • Aswath Damodaran — The Promise and Peril of Real Options — Scoped author-hosted discussion of operating option applications and cautions concerning nontraded underlying assets, exercise delays and uncertain exclusivity. No continuous-time option formula, historical company valuation or source exercise is reused.
  • Scott Schmidler / Duke — Value of Information, Statistical Decision Analysis — Finite-state perfect/imperfect information value and nonlinear-utility information-fee treatment.
